about.heading: A currency converter, built as a service.
purpose: Currency Converter turns an amount in one currency into another using Monobank’s published exchange rates. It exists to show a small service built the way a production service is built: a domain that does not know what a database is, a cache that can fail without taking the request down with it, one error shape for every failure, and a client that tells you where each number came from.
The design was written down first, in docs/architecture.md, and that document is the contract: a change to behaviour changes it in the same pull request.

status.title: Where it stands
items: Everything below is merged on main and deployed; there is nothing outstanding and no branch waiting. Every change landed through a pull request into main, each carrying review comments anchored to the lines they concern and a round of commits answering them before the author merged it with CI green. GitHub does not allow approving your own pull request, so the record is those comments and the fixes rather than an approval decision; nothing was pushed to main directly.

Every module the architecture describes is in: rates behind a cache, a stale fallback and a daily snapshot archive, conversion through three strategies, currencies, history, the health endpoints and this client.

The API and this client are two independent images, built by one CI workflow that runs lint, formatting, typecheck, tests with coverage thresholds, the build and the image build per app — plus a job that validates the shared conversion fixtures, boots the whole Docker Compose stack, probes it, and runs the integration suites against the Redis and MongoDB it started.
Both run on Railway behind the platform edge, each on its own hostname; the panel above reads the live health endpoint every 30 seconds.

This client is three pages: the converter, with searchable currency pickers and the archived rate history for the pair it is on; this reviewer page; and an operations page at /ops holding the health report, the rate snapshot and cache invalidation behind a confirmation.

All four suites pass — API unit, API end-to-end, the integration suites against a real Redis and MongoDB, and this client — with coverage gates of 85% on the API and 90% here. The counts are in the Process section below, where they carry the date they were taken.

points.description: REST endpoints under /api/v1 for convert, rates, currencies and history, documented with Swagger at /docs, plus a terminus health endpoint reporting the Redis, MongoDB and Monobank indicators. A separate /health/live answers whenever the process can serve a request, so a degraded dependency never fails a deploy gate.

The domain depends on RatesProvider, RatesRepository and HistoryRepository interfaces bound through DI tokens. Monobank, Redis and Mongo are adapters behind them, so changing the rate source or the cache is a module binding, not a rewrite.
Identity, direct pair and cross rate through UAH, selected by a resolver at request time. Amounts are computed with big.js and rounded half-up; floating point never touches money.

Each successful upstream fetch writes a fresh key (five minutes) and a fallback key (24 hours) in Redis. Concurrent misses share one in-flight call, so a burst of traffic produces a single request to Monobank.

A per-request timeout, retry with exponential backoff and full jitter, and an in-house circuit breaker (CLOSED → OPEN → HALF_OPEN) whose state feeds the health endpoint. 429 is never retried: Monobank allows one request a minute.

A small hierarchy of domain errors normalised by a global exception filter into { statusCode, code, message, details } with a timestamp, path and request id. /health is the one exception: it answers with the terminus report so a caller can see which dependency is down.

Redis or Mongo being down is logged, surfaced on /health, and reported on the answer itself as a warning — without failing the conversion. When Monobank is unreachable the response is served from the fallback snapshot and says so.

pino request logging with a request id, environment validated by a zod schema at boot, a multi-stage Docker image per app, and GitHub Actions running lint, formatting, typecheck, tests with coverage thresholds, build and the image build — one job per app, both gated on the same checks.

points.term: One set of numbers, checked on both sides
points.description: The offline estimate re-implements the server's pricing rules in the browser, so the two are held to one shared fixture set: a rates snapshot and twelve golden conversions of it, asserted by the API's end-to-end suite over HTTP and by this client's tests in the browser copy. The published OpenAPI document is committed and regenerated by a test, and every response fixture this suite renders is validated against it, so a client type that drifts from the API fails here rather than in a browser.

React 19, Vite, TanStack Query and Tailwind v4 with a dark-aware token palette. Components depend on service interfaces, never on HTTP; every string comes from an i18n dictionary, and a key that is not in that dictionary fails the typecheck. Vitest and Testing Library cover the services, the amount field, the form, the result card, the history panel and the offline estimate.

fallback.title: Two-layer fallback
paragraphs: Two different things can be down, and each has its own answer. When Monobank is unreachable the API converts from the last good snapshot it kept in Redis and labels the response stale cache, so a request still gets a number and the number still says where it came from. When the API itself is unreachable, this client converts from the rate snapshot and currency list it persisted in the browser, applying the same rules from §5 with the same big.js arithmetic, and labels the result an offline estimate with the age of the rates it used. Anything the API can answer — a validation error, an unsupported currency, no rate path — is left as the API answered it, and an estimate is never added to the history, because history is the list of what the API actually converted.

Try it: load the page once so the snapshot is saved, then stop the API — or set the Network tab in devtools to Offline — and convert again. The result comes back badged as an offline estimate instead of as an error, and it says how old the rates behind it are.

points.description: Depending on ports keeps the conversion rules testable without Redis, Mongo or the network, and it keeps infrastructure concerns from leaking into the part of the code that has the actual business rules in it. The client does the same thing: components take a service interface, and the tests hand them an in-memory one.

TanStack Query owns server state (with persistence for rates and currencies); React context provides the service implementations (swapped for fakes in tests); form state is local to the converter; there is no global store because no client state is shared beyond the query cache.

points.term: Three strategies instead of one branch
points.description: Identity, direct and cross are three different rules with three different failure modes. Keeping them apart keeps each one small and lets the API report which one it used — the strategy badge on the converter is that decision, surfaced.

Monobank rate-limits to one request a minute and does go down. An hour-old snapshot is more useful than a 503, as long as the response admits which one you are looking at. That is what the source badge is for.

points.term: Two layers of fallback, not one
points.description: Monobank being down and the API being down are different outages with different answers. The API keeps a stale snapshot in Redis; the browser keeps a persisted one of its own. Each says which it used rather than pretending the number is fresh — the section above walks through both.

points.term: Third fallback tier: an archived daily snapshot in MongoDB with a 90-day TTL
points.description: When both Monobank and the 24-hour Redis fallback are gone, the API answers from the last archived day and labels it archive with the snapshot date, so a day-old number is never mistaken for a live one. The same archive is what the rate-history panel reads, one point per day, and the TTL is why it shows at most 90.

points.term: A warning is not an error
points.description: When the cache cannot be reached, or a conversion cannot be recorded, the request still has an answer — so it gets one, with a warnings entry saying what it cost. The field is absent rather than empty when nothing degraded, so it exists to be noticed. Before this, that cost was visible only in the logs.

points.term: Liveness and readiness are different questions
points.description: /health is the dependency report and answers 503 the moment an indicator is down, which is what monitoring needs. /health/live has no indicators at all, and it is what the deploy gate, the container healthcheck and Compose probe. Pointing a rollout at /health would make Redis a hard dependency of a service that converts perfectly well without it.

nginx serves the SPA and nothing else — it proxies no API route. Each service is published by the platform edge under its own hostname, and the API restricts CORS to the web origin, which is the check a gateway would have been added to perform. One hop fewer to configure, secure and debug, and the browser talks to the API it is told about at runtime rather than to a path that happens to be rewritten.

points.term: Fail fast on config, degrade slowly at runtime
points.description: Invalid environment stops the process at boot, where the mistake is cheap to notice. A dependency dying at runtime only removes the feature that needs it, and the health endpoint names it.

A single envelope means the client renders every failure through one component, mapping the code to a translated message. VALIDATION_ERROR carries per-field messages, and the converter routes the ones it recognises back onto the matching input.

A Vite build bakes env vars into the bundle. Reading window.__APP_CONFIG__ from config.js, rewritten by the container at start, means the same image runs locally and on a hosted environment with one variable changed.

points.term: A fourth tier behind the cache
points.description: Redis holds a fresh key and a stale one, and both expire. Behind them MongoDB keeps one rate snapshot per UTC day, so an outage longer than the stale key still has an answer — dated to a day rather than to a minute, refused past a configured age, and labelled as the archive it came from. It is also the series the rate history reads.

points.term: A picker you can type into
points.description: A native select over 180 currencies is a list nobody reads to the end, so each picker is a combobox: a trigger that opens a search, matching on the code first and the name second, with the matched letters marked in the row. It is a popover under the trigger on a wide screen and a modal bottom sheet on a phone, because a sheet is what a thumb reaches and what the platform lets you dismiss.

points.term: An operations page, not a curl command
points.description: Everything the API says about itself, on one page: the health report on a 30-second poll, the rate snapshot with the two cache windows worked out in the browser and said on its face to be derived, and the cache invalidation behind a confirmation. The admin key stays in the tab's memory for as long as the tab lives and is never stored — one shared key with no identity behind it is a demo convenience rather than an operator console.

The fourth tier is already a day-by-day series, so the panel beside the converter plots it for the pair on screen — an inline chart with no charting dependency, and the same days as a table beside it for a reader who wants the numbers. An answer priced from that archive says so with its own source badge and the day it was recorded.

Light, dark and system, persisted, with system following the OS. Every colour is a token defined once and redefined per theme, so no component names one and a third theme is a block of variables rather than a pass over the components.

howToRun.title: How to run it
howToRun.intro: Two commands from the repository root bring up the whole thing. The README has the rest — per-app scripts, port overrides and the deploy.

blocks.caption: Backing services in Docker, both apps from npm

notes: npm run dev waits for Redis and MongoDB to report healthy, then runs the API on :3000 and the Vite dev server on :5173 side by side. docker compose up --build serves the built client on :8080 instead, with the API still on :3000.

Neither needs a secret or an account: every environment variable has a default, and the one the production schema insists on — the admin key for cache invalidation — has a local placeholder in the Compose file.
This client reads its API URL from public/config.js at runtime, so pointing it at another API needs no rebuild — the container rewrites that file from API_URL at start.

traceability.title: Requirements, and where each one is
traceability.intro: The task was eight numbered sections. Each is met; the README carries the full table, one row per atom with the file, the test name and the live URL behind it.

points.description: NestJS 11 on Node 24, TypeScript strict. Repository: two ports with adapters for Redis and Mongo, bound by DI token. Dependency injection: seven tokens, and every unit test substitutes a fake through the one the runtime uses. Strategy: identity, direct pair and cross via UAH, ordered as data in the module and picked by a resolver that contains no per-strategy branch.

POST /api/v1/convert takes from, to and amount. Codes are case-insensitive and echoed upper-cased; amount has to be a JSON number, so "100" is a 400 naming the field rather than a value quietly reinterpreted.

points.term: 3. Fetching from Monobank, with error handling
points.description: A provider that validates the upstream payload with zod at the boundary, retries network errors and 5xx with exponential backoff and full jitter, never retries a 429, and runs inside a hand-written circuit breaker under a total time budget. No upstream URL, status text or body ever reaches a client.

Redis cache-aside: a fresh key on a configurable TTL and a long-lived fallback key, written together, with concurrent misses sharing one upstream call. Invalidation is both the TTL and DELETE /api/v1/rates/cache behind an API key.

One snapshot per conversion, so two legs cannot straddle a cache expiry. Cross rates compose the leg into the hryvnia with the leg out of it and pay the spread twice. All arithmetic is big.js on a private constructor; the rate is published rounded to six decimals while the result is computed from the unrounded one.

One envelope for every failure, produced by a global exception filter, with a request id echoed on the response and on every log line for it. Validation reports one message per field. Unsupported currency and no-rate-path are distinct codes. Rates, history and cache each have their own 503. A cache failure on a read is reported as a warning on the answer that still succeeded, and on the invalidation route as a 503, because there success would be a lie.

One Compose file for api, web, Redis and Mongo, healthchecks on all four and the API waiting on the other two. A dev overlay runs the backing services alone for the npm path. CI boots the full stack on every pull request and probes it.

A README with three ways to run it, the whole configuration surface and one curl per endpoint with the response it actually returns; Swagger generated from the code and kept in step by a test that fails on a route documented but not served; the architecture document behind both.

process.title: Process
paragraphs: Specification first. docs/architecture.md was written before any implementation code and describes the module layout, the API contract, the caching and resilience model, the error envelope and the testing strategy. Every pull request was reviewed against it, and behaviour that changed changed the document in the same pull request.

Then one pull request at a time, every change landing in main that way. Each drew review comments anchored to the lines they concern and a round of commits answering them, and was merged by its author with CI green: lint, formatting, typecheck, build, unit tests against coverage thresholds, the API end-to-end suite, both Docker images, and a job that starts the whole Compose stack and probes it. GitHub does not allow approving your own pull request, so what the record shows is those comments and the commits that answered them rather than an approval decision; nothing was pushed to main directly.

The implementation was AI-assisted, under human direction and review: the architecture, the scope of each pull request and the decisions listed above were set and reviewed by a person, and coding agents wrote the code against them. The commits carry a Co-Authored-By trailer saying so, so the record is in the git history rather than in a claim on this page.

stages.title: In stages
items: The architecture contract, written and committed before any implementation code.
The API and this client built in parallel against that contract, rather than against each other.
Stacked feature pull requests: rates with its cache and circuit breaker, then conversion, then history.
The offline fallback, then a UX pass over the form it answers on.
Polish, documentation and a consolidation pass that put both implementations of the pricing rules on one shared fixture set, then naming conventions and lint-enforced module boundaries.
The rate archive as a fourth lookup tier, and a design pass drawn on a Claude Design canvas and implemented as three redesign pull requests.
Read-only audits over the merged result, each opening a pull request only where it found something.

numbers.title: By the numbers
numbers.caption: As of 9 September 2026, with the last redesign pull request and the one adding this section still open — so every row moves when they land. The rest of this page is written without counts so it stays true as they do; these carry a date instead.

rows.metric: Pull requests that went back for a fix round

examples.title: Five things the review caught
examples.intro: Each was reproduced before it was reported, and each is a line-anchored comment on the pull request that introduced the code.

points.term: Redis rejected its own first command
points.description: A lazy connection with the offline queue disabled and no eager connect meant the first command after boot rejected against a healthy Redis. Every cold start would have missed the cache and failed its first save. Fixed by connecting on module init and keeping the offline queue disabled for the genuinely-down case.

points.term: The offline cache erased itself when it was needed
points.description: The persister kept only queries whose latest fetch had succeeded, and it rewrites the whole store on every cache event — so the first unreachable refetch emptied the snapshot the fallback exists to read. Measured at 15 KB to empty. Fixed by keeping any query that still holds data.

points.term: The two implementations of the pricing rules had drifted
points.description: The API and the browser each carried their own copy of the rates table, and the copies disagreed on two of five pairs — so both suites were green about different numbers. Both now read one shared snapshot and assert the same golden conversions, which a script re-prices independently.

points.term: A dangling decimal separator and Enter failed validation
points.description: The amount field trimmed a trailing separator on blur, and Enter submits without blurring — the primary path on a phone. The same thread turned up the worse case behind it: under a locale that groups with a full stop, a thousands separator parsed as a decimal one, a silent thousandfold error. Both closed by canonicalising the value on submit.

points.term: A test that could not fail
points.description: The Mongo integration suite seeded one row and asserted one row back, so it passed with and without the limit clamp it claimed to cover — verified by deleting the clamp and watching it stay green. Reseeded past the maximum, it fails without it.

process.linkIntro: The whole record — the stages, the loop, the audits, the roles, and the honest limits of a process reviewed by agents rather than by a second person — is in the repository.

snapshot.title: Rate snapshot · GET /api/v1/rates
snapshot.note: {{count}} currencies, every pair crossed through UAH. Monobank allows one request a minute; a burst of misses shares one upstream call.
snapshot.derived: Both expiries are worked out in this browser from the fetch time and the TTLs in the architecture document (5 min, 24 h); the API publishes neither.
snapshot.unavailable: The rate snapshot could not be read, so there is nothing to say about the cache keys.

clear.title: Clear the rates cache
clear.description: Drops both keys. The next conversion refetches from Monobank.
clear.confirmBody: Both the fresh key and the 24-hour fallback are dropped. Until the next fetch succeeds there is no snapshot to fall back on — if Monobank is unreachable, conversions answer 503 RATES_UNAVAILABLE.
clear.success: Cache cleared. The next conversion fetches from Monobank.
clear.staleWarning: Clearing now would leave nothing to fall back on while Monobank is unreachable.

actions.title: Actions this session
actions.empty: Nothing has been sent from this page yet.

health.unreachable: The health endpoint did not answer.

warnings.CACHE_UNAVAILABLE: The rates cache could not be reached, so these rates came straight from Monobank and were not cached for the next request.
warnings.HISTORY_NOT_RECORDED: This conversion was answered but could not be saved, so it will not appear under recent conversions.
warnings.ARCHIVE_NOT_RECORDED: The rates behind this answer were fetched but could not be archived, so that day will be missing from the rate history and cannot back a later fallback.

errors.fieldErrorsLead: Fix the following and try again.

codes.VALIDATION_ERROR: The request did not pass validation.
codes.UNAUTHORIZED: This request needs an admin API key.
codes.NOT_FOUND: The API does not have that endpoint.
codes.UNSUPPORTED_CURRENCY: That currency is not in the current rate snapshot.
codes.RATE_NOT_AVAILABLE: No rate path connects those two currencies right now.
codes.TOO_MANY_REQUESTS: Too many requests. Wait a moment and try again.
codes.RATES_UNAVAILABLE: Exchange rates are unavailable: Monobank could not be reached and there is no recent snapshot to fall back on.
codes.CACHE_UNAVAILABLE: The rates cache could not be reached, so it could not be cleared.
codes.HISTORY_UNAVAILABLE: Recent conversions cannot be read right now: the history store is unreachable.
codes.ARCHIVE_UNAVAILABLE: Rate history cannot be read right now: the rate archive is unreachable.
codes.INTERNAL_ERROR: The API failed unexpectedly. Try again in a moment.
codes.NETWORK_ERROR: Cannot reach the API at {{url}}. Check that it is running and reachable.
